title: Harvesting Rights, Section 35, and Careful Claims
intro: The rights test courts actually apply. Question 80 is answered in this lesson — your writing saves here; question 79 needs the textbook.

terms.def: The court's three-part check: the activity is integral to the group's distinctiveness, was practised before contact or Crown control, and continues in modern form.

body: For an Aboriginal group to use resources in a modern way, the practice must pass the rights test: integral to the group's distinctiveness as a society, exercised before contact or effective Crown control, and still practised, even in changed form. Title claims are rooted in land while rights claims are rooted in activities.

A caution: the teacher key answers a different question than question 79 asks, so do not trust a remembered answer here. Read textbook pages 86-89 directly and answer exactly what question 79 states about hunting, fishing, and trapping.

The rights test itself is fully teachable and fully tested. Part one asks whether the activity sits at the core of who the people are. Part two asks whether it predates contact or effective Crown control. Part three asks whether it continues, even transformed by new tools. Modern fishing with new gear passes when all three hold; any failure ends the claim.

Notice how the test protects change. Requiring modern form alongside ancient roots means peoples may adopt motors, rifles, and markets without forfeiting rights. Continuity of purpose counts, not frozen technique.

example.title: Worked application
example.text: Take modern fishing with new gear. Ask the three test questions: integral to distinctiveness, pre-contact roots, and continuing practice. If all three hold, the modern form is protected.

check.prompt: What are the three parts of the rights test?
check.sample: Sample response: integral to distinctiveness, rooted before contact or Crown control, and still practised in modern form.

title: Rebuilding Self-Government: Goals and Negotiations
intro: Why one size cannot fit all, and who sits at the table. Begin Assignment 1.2 here.

terms.def: Aboriginal control over matters affecting Aboriginal communities, negotiated nation by nation because no single model fits all.
Self-government deals negotiated by three partners: the federal government, a province or territory, and one or more Aboriginal governments.

body: No single model fits because nations differ in land, population, history, and goals, which is why agreements are negotiated nation by nation. Today's deals are generally tripartite: federal, provincial or territorial, and Aboriginal governments together, each with its own mandate that can snag the talks.

The federal response pledged to fully implement treaty terms, strengthen self-government, fund Aboriginal governments, and design development programs jointly. Assignment 1.2 asks you to choose one of the four page-98 advantages and argue why it would help a First Nation; collect your example now and write after Lesson 22.

Tripartite structure explains why talks stall as often as they advance. Three partners means three mandates, three electorates, and three definitions of success, with provinces guarding jurisdiction and Ottawa guarding the treasury while nations guard the future. Deadlock usually signals mandate conflict, not bad faith.

One size fails for the opposite reason: nations differ in land, population, history, and goals. An urban First Nation without a land base needs different tools than a treaty nation with territory, which is why the models lesson follows and why Assignment 1.2 rewards matching the advantage to a real nation's situation.

example.title: Assignment 1.2 starts here
example.text: List the four advantages from textbook page 98, pick the one you can best evidence from Lessons 17-22, and note one example beside it before writing.

check.prompt: Who are the three partners in self-government negotiations?
check.sample: Sample response: the federal government, a provincial or territorial government, and one or more Aboriginal governments.

title: Comparing Models of Self-Government
intro: Protection, public government, and municipal models side by side. Complete Assignment 1.2 after this lesson.

terms.def: A government all residents elect, as in Nunavut, where an Aboriginal majority keeps it rooted in Inuit culture and values.
Self-government by legislation, first for the Cree of Northern Quebec in 1984, then the Sechelt Indian Band in 1986 with powers over education, health, and more.

body: Enshrining self-government in the Constitution matters because leaders now build on Section 35's foundation through courts and negotiations instead of chasing new amendments. Nunavut shows the public model: all residents vote, and the Inuit majority keeps government rooted in Inuit culture, opened in 2004 when Elder Enoapik Sageatok lit the qulliq.

The municipal route runs on legislation. The Cree of Northern Quebec came first in 1984, and Bill C-43 created the Sechelt Indian government district in 1986 with broad powers. Urban First Nations without a land base fit neither classic model, which is why the chapter treats urban government as its own design problem.

Enshrining matters because foundations decide fights. With Section 35 in place, leaders build through courts applying the rights test and negotiations applying tripartite mandates, instead of begging amendments from governments that benefit from the status quo. Protection first, then construction.

Nunavut's opening tells the public model in one image: in 2004 an Elder lit the qulliq, the traditional oil lamp, to open a government every resident elects. Majority Inuit demographics keep that government rooted in Inuit culture and values without excluding anyone, which is the public model's whole argument.

example.title: Assignment 1.2 due now
example.text: Write the Assignment 1.2 response now: one page-98 advantage, why it would help a First Nation, one example from Lessons 17-22, and an honest limit. Do not add a second essay or fresh legal research.

check.prompt: Compare public and municipal-style government in one sentence each.
check.sample: Sample response: public government elects everyone with an Aboriginal majority shaping it, as in Nunavut; municipal-style government arrives by legislation with defined powers, as with the Cree in 1984 and Sechelt in 1986.
